Their aim was mischief, and while I true patriots, such as Henry Grattan were I urgently trying to introduce reforms by con- stitutional means, these mis-guided men , were in personal communication with the! French Directory, and were arranging with! the French General for a descent upon Ire- land. Meanwhile the old dominant faction, : whose only principles of Government were ' Protestant aeoentiancy.patronage,and bribery were necessarily opposed to every measured, chumessiou and reform; while, strange contradiction! the "patriots" were equally I impatient at the removal of any particular :cause of discontent, and of any policy that " would bind the union with Great Britain. I The accession to office of the Duke of Port- ' I load and his friends, in 1704, afforded 01,- portunity for change. The Viceroy, Lord Westmoreland, was entirely in the hands of! the old corrupt party; it was proposed that • I he should be removed from the lieutenancy,, land that a successor should be sent over to form other connections, and introduce ' 'another policy. Pitt strenuously opposed the, being averse to any change of system or placemen. The premier's wish, after much debate, was accepted, and, to lessen the dif- ficulty the Lord President, Earl Fitzwilliam, the great Whig landowner, himself offered to accept the difficult post. There could not' have been a better selection. Lord Fitz- wilkam —primer Mt.r porn—was an ardent reformer, and sincerely hoped to do justice to Ireland. He told ,Grattan that the Go- ' aernment could not at present introduce a limn for Catholic emancipation, but clearly lett it upon his mind that he would be glad if Grattan would introduce it as his own I measure. Grattan took the hint, and when I Lord Fitzwilliam arrived in Dublin at the close of 1794, loyal and congratulatory ad. I dresses poured in from all parts of the island; the Roman Catholics went in an im- posing proceasion to the castle to present an address, in which they expressed the hope that their friends would had a place in his Excellency's councils. The Lord Lieu- tenant's reply did not discourage this ex- ontion. The Irish Parliament was opened -o Grattan

en 22nd January, 1795, who.. moved the address; and in a few days, and at the Lord Lieutenant's request, brought in a bill repealing absolutely and immedi- ately all the penalties and disabilities affect- ing Eoman Catholics. The bill had been prepared tr ith the Viceroy's sanction, and communicated by him to the Cabinet in London before it was presented to the Irish Parliament. It was not till the Bth of February that the Duke of Portland wrote to the Lord Lieutenant urging him in the strongest terms neither to commit himself by any engagements, nor even by words Ito the Catholic measure, The command was I as startling an it was unwelcome ; but the cause was not far to seek. Lord Fitzwilliam was a reformer in more senses than one. Ile founds mass of jobbery and corruption that was truly appaling, and he was determined to diminish, if he could not abolish it. He wished to dismiss nuch obscure placemen as Vs olfe and Toler from the Attorney and Soli- tor Generalship, and appoint to these posts Ponamby, the first debater in the Commons, and Curran, the most elo- quent advocate in the Four Courta.l lie made other ministerial change.. But he had more formidable work before him. The most powerful family in Ireland was that of Berenford, and he had the misfortune to I rouse the opposition of its chief immediately after his arrival. This person was Commis- sioner of Eevenue, a not very important , office, but his influence was so great that I Fitzwilliam called him King of Ireland. One of his first acts was to dismiss Beret. ford from his employment. This spread the utmost consternation among, and raised the opposition of the place-hunters. The Vice- roy had also insisted on the removal of the Chancellor, Lord Fitzgibbon, as a condition of his undertaking the government of Ire- land. Ile had thus the two moat vwerful men, as well as a number of inferior per. eons, arrayed against him. Complaints were made to the Cabinet, but it is probable that I Pitt would have passed them by unheeded. I Fitzgibbon was equal to the occasion, and carried hie complaint to the King, telling I him that emancipation would be incompat- ible with the connection between Great Britain and Ireland ; that it would, in fact, be a violation of the coronation oath. The King took the opinion of his Chief Justice Kenyon, a man as narrow and bigoted as his master. Kenyon's answer was evasive, leaving the King to act as he thought beet. The result was immediate and disastrous the Lord Chancellor was raised to the Earl- dom of Clare, and Fitzwilliam was recalled. itt appointed Lord Camden in his place ; but his entry, on the 31et March, was marked by a gloomy silence. When the Officers of butte waited upon the new Viceroy at the Castle, the rage of the populace was un- governable. Beresford'a house was attacked by a furious mob, which had to be dispersed by- he militaryc and the Chancellor, at- tacked in his carriage, nearly lost his life. The people were no humour to be pro- pitiated. "Their hope isad been raised high," says Mr. Massey, „ the;-..,74 ber taught to think that justice was at last to on aone to their country ; that the days of pub- lic robbery and monopoly ware numbered; ,118 t all raoa wore 19 lto opal P9iOTO the

Before the L dt of the moat it became known most popular Governor who had ever occupied the Caetia was to be hastily removed because he was about to do justice to Ireland. The excite- ment throughout the country wits intense. Both houses of Parliament passed unani- mous votes of confidence in the Lord-Lieu- tenant. blinder resolutions were agreed to by most of the corporate bodies, many of the oouuties, and numerous public assemblies. The day on which Fitzwilliem quitted Ire- land, was a day of gloom, and a day of evil omen whioh has hardly yet been fallilled. On that day the Irish people abandoned all further hope that tho policy of 1782 was to be resumed and carried into effect. The Presbyteriane of the north, who cherished the traditions of English liberty, and the Boman Catholic body, who pined for reli- gious freedom, were now ready to unite in a , common cause againet a common foe. Even that party, never very numerous in Ireland, though comprining the best friends of their , country, who sought to obtain both civil and religious liberty by legal and coustitutional means, began to hold different language. Somerset House, during the last few days, has paid a compliment to the borough of I Warrington, the like of which has not tosei- bly been received by any industrial mai- muni,y in the British islands. The sanitary literature of England has for many years past been growing in volume and importance, and it is not too much to say that some of the best minds of the country have been dedicated to the consideration of , questions nearly concerning the phyeical I welfare of our vast industrial popu- lation. The cloud which has overhung the marvellous proeperity of England, acid obscured a brightness which otherwise would have cast a eiagular lustre over the history of the nineteenth century, has been on- I doubtedly the heavy urban mortality which seems to have been the price—the dismal: price—whioh the country has had to pay for it. There are few of our great industrial' centres where British labour molt doth eon- I gregato, where the weekly, or quarterly, or annual table of mortality, does not disclose figuree, pregnant with a story of physical misery which strikes the benevolent and the reflective mind with melancholy sadness, It is indeed a striking circumstance in the his- tory of this borough that the general health of Ito inhabitants and ite freedom from fatal disease is so extraordinary, that the rate of mortality in the borough is: so exeeptionally low, that it has excited the surprise and curiosity of the authorities at Somerset Bourne to such a degree that the Registrar General has just addressed an in. to Dr. Joseph, the accomplished officer of health for the borough, Raking to be informed of the causee to which this extraordinary immunity from fatal disease is to be attributed. the communication ad- I dressed to Dr. Joseph by the secretary of the Registrar-General is flitted from the General Registry Office, Somerset 'louse, on the 20th inst., and ie couched in the following term,: " I am requested by Dr. Fan to ask if you will kindly oblige him by stating what, in your oplnion, has been the cause of the de- crease in the death rate of the district of Warrington in the five years 1871-6. It ap- pears that the average annual rate of mor- tality for each thousand of the population for the district of Warrington was, for 1851-60, 24 : for 1861-70, 26: and 1871-74, 23" ! The reduction in the death rate is so signal and exceptional that Dr. Joseph is invited to "state if any sanitary works are in pro- gress " The inquiry is perfectly natural, and it reflects credit on the authorities in London that they are anxious tubs put in pos.: seasion of the secret—if there be one—of this remarkable and enviable sanitary condition. We are not, at this moment in a position to disclose the terms of the reply which our officer of Health will doubtless feel it his duty to communicate to the Registrar- General, but it will not be improper to in- dicate in general terms, that Dr. Joseph will do but justice in ascribing the excep- tional sanitary condition of Warrington, to an intelligent and vigilant zeal on the part of the Corporation, and especially to the Health Committee of our municipal body. It is but an act of common fairness to claim for the Corporation of Warrington —oast and present—an assiduity and swiss ~-,,, ..x.yendi!ure in all matters reit:, liberality. she inhabitants of the ting to the heath -•- beough, gat 11141 lot prebtlil
